new_sources.summary: This paper explores the notion of personal missionary presence as the determining factor in interreligious encounters and relationships. The attitude and conduct of a missionary in relationship with potential and actual converts greatly influences their response to that missionary's teachings. In turn, the converts’ overall understanding (or misunderstanding) of the missionary's faith is shaped by the conduct of the missionary. To illustrate this proposition, the article discusses the vocation of Max Warren (1904–77), one of the most influential British missiologists of the twentieth century. Warren, a son of British missionaries, was brought up for the first eight years of his life in India
new_sources.title: Missionary Presence in Interreligious Encounters and Relationships

new_sources.summary: Background Older adults' low adoption of healthcare robots indicates that their lived processes of acceptance remain insufficiently understood. This gap is not merely technical but also ethical, involving questions of dignity, relational integrity, and autonomy in later life. This study aimed to develop a theory-grounded framework of how older adults pragmatically evaluate healthcare robots in home-based aging contexts, with particular attention to the ethical and relational considerations shaping their acceptance decisions. new_sources.title: A conceptual framework for pragmatic acceptance of healthcare robots among older adults: a computational grounded theory.
